TITLE: Adapting Sampling Temperature in Critic-Free LLM RL
PROPOSAL: We adapt existing critic-free RL algorithms (e.g., REINFORCE++, DAPO) to treat the sampling temperature as a decision variable that can be optimized through self-supervised meta-learning. During training, we extract the trajectories' rewards and performance metrics (e.g., perplexity, BLEU score) and use them to guide an external meta-learner that produces a temporal schedule for adjusting the temperature. The goal is to adaptively balance exploration and exploitation throughout the learning process.
CONTROLS: Compare with two baselines: (1) the standard version of the chosen critic-free algorithm without temperature adaptation, and (2) a variant using a static temperature schedule (heuristically chosen or annealing-based). We also consider two ablations: (1) a simpler meta-learner (e.g., linear model) and (2) an annealing-based temperature schedule without meta-learning.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect temperature adaptation to lead to improved policy performance, especially in the context of mathematical reasoning, where exploration is crucial for stumbling upon novel theorems or mathematical structures. Potential failure could stem from the meta-learner's inability to capture relevant signal from the trajectory data or from the algorithm's inability to maintain stability under adaptive temperature changes.

Specifically, we will use a moving window of past performances and adjust the temperature adaptation signals to favor convergence and stable performance during early stages of training. This should help to prevent temperature adaptation from inducing instability in the policy.

TITLE: Evaluating the Transferability of Temperature Adaptation across Different Task Domains
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the transferability of temperature adaptation across different task domains in LLM RL, by testing the performance of models trained with temperature adaptation on unseen tasks. Specifically, we will use a set of tasks from mathematical reasoning and commonsense question answering, and evaluate the performance of models trained with temperature adaptation on these tasks. This will provide insight into the potential applicability of temperature adaptation to different task domains.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original temperature adaptation proposals, using the same baselines. We also consider an ablation without temperature adaptation.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the evaluation to reveal that temperature adaptation improves transferability across task domains, especially in LLM RL. Potential failure could arise from the temperature adaptation mechanism being overly task-specific, or from the difficulty in generalizing across different task domains.

This proposal is focused on evaluating the potential benefits of temperature adaptation in a more general sense, by testing its transferability across different task domains.

TITLE: Online Temperature Adaptation via Meta-Gradient Learning
PROPOSAL: We will use meta-gradient learning to adapt the sampling temperature online during LLM reinforcement learning. We will add a meta-temperature variable to the policy and compute meta-gradients w.r.t. this variable, using a simplified critic-free RL algorithm, such as REINFORCE++. This approach treats temperature as a trainable decision variable, allowing it to adapt to the changing demands of RL during training.
CONTROLS: REINFORCE++ as baseline, ablations will use fixed temperature and manual tuning of temperature
COST: 30 GPU-hours (meta-gradient computation is relatively inexpensive)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in policy quality, especially in tasks that require exploration, and reduced computational overhead due to dynamic temperature adaptation. However, high variance in meta-gradient estimates might lead to inconsistent temperature updates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Label-Sensitive Temperature Adaptation for Commonsense Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with applying the online temperature adaptation mechanism (proposed in proposal 1) specifically to the task of Commonsense Question Answering (CQA). We will investigate whether adapting the sampling temperature based on feedback from the training trajectories leads to better performance on CQA benchmarks, as well as in mathematical reasoning tasks. We will use a pre-trained LLM and a set of carefully selected CQA and mathematical reasoning tasks from the benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 as baseline, with ablations using fixed temperature and manual tuning of temperature, and a separate set of experiments using a non-adaptive entropy regularization schedule
COST: 50 GPU-hours (largely due to the need to retrain the LLM on the CQA and reasoning tasks)
PREDICTION: We expect to see a lift in performance on CQA and reasoning tasks when using label-sensitive temperature adaptation, as the mechanism can better calibrate exploration to the characteristics of the task at hand, such as handling open-ended questions and reasoning queries.

TITLE: REVISED Label-Sensitive Temperature Adaptation for Commonsense Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will revise the proposal 2 to include an evaluation protocol that assesses the impact of temperature adaptation on both diversity and accuracy in generated responses. To this end, we will modify the temperature adaptation mechanism to optimize a multi-objective loss function, which simultaneously rewards high accuracy and high response diversity. We will evaluate the trade-offs between these objectives using qualitative and quantitative methods.
CONTROLS: Same as before, but with modifications to the evaluation protocol
COST: No change in estimated cost (aldy 50 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: We expect to see a nuanced understanding of how label-sensitive temperature adaptation affects the trade-off between diversity and accuracy. Specifically, we predict that this approach will lead to a significant increase in diversity without sacrificing accuracy, or may find a sweet spot where the two objectives converge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Online Temperature Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a thorough investigation into the robustness of the online temperature adaptation mechanism to different types of noise and perturbations in the training signals. We will train the LLM on CQA and reasoning tasks with various levels of noise injection and assess the stability and adaptability of the temperature adaptation mechanism. This will help identify potential vulnerabilities and limitations of the approach.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 as baseline, ablations using fixed temperature and manual tuning of temperature, as well as scenarios with different noise injection levels
COST: 70 GPU-hours (due to the need for multiple noise injection scenarios and retraining the LLM)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the online temperature adaptation mechanism is generally robust to moderate levels of noise and perturbations, but may be vulnerable to more extreme scenarios. This understanding will inform the design of more robust and adaptive temperature adaptation mechanisms.

TITLE: Comparing Online Temperature Adaptation to Alternative Exploration Strategies
PROPOSAL: We will explore the performance of online temperature adaptation in comparison to alternative exploration strategies, including entropy regularization and nucleus sampling. We will implement a set of ablations that apply each of these exploration strategies to the CQA and reasoning tasks and evaluate their performance in comparison to the online temperature adaptation mechanism.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 as baseline, with ablations using entropy regularization, nucleus sampling, and other exploration strategies
COST: 40 GPU-hours (due to the need to implement and evaluate multiple exploration strategies)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that online temperature adaptation performs competitively with other exploration strategies, but may demonstrate advantages in specific task regimes or under certain noise levels. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the approach.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate the feasibility and benefits of implementing online temperature adaptation in large-scale RL pipelines with real-world data and compute constraints. We will select a representative dataset and a robust implementation of the online temperature adaptation mechanism and assess its performance in this setting.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 as baseline, with ablations using fixed temperature and manual tuning of temperature

PREDICTION: We expect to see that online temperature adaptation can be successfully deployed in large-scale RL pipelines, with potential improvements in policy quality and exploration efficiency, although the lift in performance may be modest due to the challenges of working with real-world data and compute constraints.

TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Online Temperature Adaptation on Policy Interpretability
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of online temperature adaptation on the interpretability of the learned policy. We will analyze the features that are most sensitive to temperature changes and the distribution of attention weights across different regions of the input. This will provide insights into how online temperature adaptation can be used to improve policy interpretability.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 as baseline, with ablations using fixed temperature and manual tuning of temperature
COST: 80 GPU-hours (due to the need to retrain models and compute interpretability metrics)
